title: Use one query inside another
description: Use IN, EXISTS, grouped subqueries, scalar counts and a CTE to build an author report.

steps.label: IN
steps.title: Use a query as the list of matching IDs
steps.body:
A **subquery** is a query inside another SQL query. This guide uses PostgreSQL and Drizzle ORM **1.0.0-rc.5**, with authors and their published or draft posts.

`publishedAuthorIds` selects one column: author IDs from published posts. Pass that query directly to `inArray`. **Do not await the inner query**: awaiting would fetch an array into JavaScript instead of composing one SQL statement.

Press **Run**. Ada and Grace appear once each, even though Ada's ID occurs twice in the inner query. `IN` checks membership; it does not join each matching post into another row.

meta.summary: Filter authors using an unawaited query that selects one column.
meta.changed: Ada and Grace returned once each; Linus did not match.

steps.label: EXISTS
steps.title: Check whether a related row exists
steps.body:
A **correlated subquery** refers to a column from its outer query. Here, `matchingPosts` compares each post's author ID with the outer author's ID.

`exists` asks whether at least one matching row exists. Its selected value does not matter. `notExists` asks the opposite, without adding child rows to the result.

Press **Run**. The first result contains Ada and Grace. The second contains Linus. If you omit the author-ID comparison, you ask whether any published post exists anywhere, which would match every author in this data.

meta.summary: Use EXISTS and NOT EXISTS without multiplying parent rows.
meta.changed: Ada and Grace have published posts; Linus has none.

steps.label: Grouped query
steps.title: Join a grouped subquery like a table
steps.body:
Now you need each author's published-post count and total views. Group posts by author ID, then name that query with `.as("published_stats")`. You can join it like a table.

Computed columns also need SQL aliases: `.as("published_count")` and `.as("total_views")` let the outer query reference them. JavaScript property names alone do not name raw SQL expressions.

Press **Run**. The left join keeps Linus, and the outer `coalesce` turns missing totals into zero. `.mapWith(Number)` converts these small aggregate values at the result boundary; `sql<number>` by itself would only describe a type.

meta.summary: Give a grouped query and its computed fields names before joining them.
meta.changed: Ada has 2 published posts and 40 views; Grace has 1 and 5; Linus has zeros.

steps.label: One value
steps.title: Select one value from a subquery
steps.body:
A **scalar subquery** supplies one column from at most one row as a value in the outer selection. This one counts published posts for the current author.

`count()` without `groupBy` produces exactly one row, including zero when no posts match. The outer selection converts that count to a JavaScript number.

Press **Run**. Ada has two, Grace one and Linus zero. An arbitrary multi-row query cannot be used here: PostgreSQL rejects a scalar subquery that returns more than one row.

meta.summary: Use a one-row, one-column subquery as a selected value.

steps.label: WITH
steps.title: Name the grouped query with a CTE
steps.body:
A **common table expression (CTE)** names a query inside a SQL statement's `WITH` clause. `db.$with("published_stats").as(...)` defines it; `db.with(publishedStats)` includes it in the statement that uses it.

This is the same grouped report as before, written with a CTE. It is not a saved table or a promise that the database materializes or caches the result.

Press **Run**. The full report is unchanged. The second query filters by at least 30 published views, leaving Ada. Grace's 100 draft views never enter the grouped totals.

displays: Authors with at least 30 published views

meta.summary: Use WITH to name a query within a statement and filter its computed totals.
meta.changed: The report matches the grouped-subquery version. Only Ada meets the 30-view threshold.

steps.label: Use the starter
steps.title: Choose the shape the outer query needs
steps.body:
Use `IN` for membership in a one-column result. Use `EXISTS` or `NOT EXISTS` when only the presence of a matching row matters. Use an aliased subquery in `FROM` or a join when you need several computed fields. Use a scalar subquery for one value, and a CTE when naming the query separately makes the statement easier to read.

These are ways to compose SQL, not a ranking of performance. Inspect the generated SQL and the database plan for your own data.

[Open the Author report starter](/examples/author-report) for the complete CTE query. For nested collections, continue with [Build nested results with SQL](/examples/nested-sql-results).

meta.summary: Choose between membership, existence, a table-shaped result and a scalar value.
